The enormous size dimorphism characteristic of Mirounga leonina is among the most extreme documented in any mammalian species. This pronounced disparity in linear dimensions is mirrored in body mass, with adult males attaining a staggering maximum wet weight of 3.5 million grams [Wwi = 3.5 million grams], while adult females plateau at a considerably more modest 400,000 grams [Wwi = 400,000 grams]. Such dramatic sexual dimorphism is thought to be driven by intense polygynous mating competition, where large male body size confers a decisive advantage in establishing and defending breeding territories.

By the time maternal provisioning ceases, offspring have achieved a wet weight at weaning of roughly 125,000 grams [Wwx = roughly 125,000 grams], representing a nearly threefold increase from their birth mass.

Female Mirounga leonina follow a comparatively slow life-history trajectory, consistent with their large body size and capital breeding strategy. Longitudinal studies tracking known individuals on Macquarie Island reveal that the time since birth at puberty for females is 1,059 days [tp = 1,059 days] when measured at the species' typical core temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This prolonged period of somatic development reflects the substantial energetic investment required to accumulate the lipid reserves necessary to support both gestation and lactation. Longevity records from tagging programs conducted at the Valdés Peninsula demonstrate that Mirounga leonina possesses an impressive lifespan, with reliable observations of individuals surviving for up to 25 years [am = up to 25 years] at a core body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This extended maximum lifespan is characteristic of large, long-lived marine mammals and is coupled with a delayed onset of reproductive activity. The developmental interval from birth to the initiation of gonadal maturation covers nearly three years, a considerable gap that reflects the substantial time required to attain the body condition necessary for successful breeding. The species' deep-diving, pelagic foraging lifestyle likely contributes to this slow-paced life history, as the energetic costs of long-distance travel and deep diving limit the frequency of breeding attempts and place a premium on individual survival and the accumulation of large body size.

Comparisons with other members of the Phocidae family contextualize the extreme growth patterns observed in the southern elephant seal. While male Li values for many true seals rarely exceed 250 cm, the 500 cm [Li = 500 cm] attained by male Mirounga leonina represents a remarkable evolutionary outlier linked to the species' uniquely polygynous social system. Similarly, the adult female mass of 400,000 grams [Wwi = 400,000 grams] places this species among the heaviest of all phocids, with females investing heavily in subcutaneous blubber layers that facilitate prolonged fasting during both lactation and molting.
